title: When Police May Arrest Without Warrant
old_text: Any police officer may without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, arrest any person who has been concerned in any cognizable offence, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received...
new_text: Any police officer may without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, arrest any person who has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years... provided that for offences punishable with imprisonment of less than three years, prior approval of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police is required for elderly/infirm persons.
punishment_old: Procedural power of arrest with Arnesh Kumar safeguards.
punishment_new: Safeguards codified into statute: prior DSP approval required for arrest in minor offences (<3 years) for elderly/infirm individuals.
explanation: CrPC Section 41 has been relocated to BNSS Section 35. Key procedural changes include statutory restrictions on arresting persons aged 60 and above or infirm persons for minor offences without DSP approval.
source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023), Section 35

title: Information in Cognizable Cases (FIR, Zero FIR & e-FIR)
chapter: Information to Police and Powers to Investigate
old_text: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant...
new_text: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, irrespective of the area where the crime was committed, may be given orally or by electronic communication (e-FIR) to an officer in charge of a police station... Provided that information given by electronic communication shall be signed within three days by the person giving it before the FIR is formally registered.
punishment_old: Statutory right to register FIR at jurisdictional police station.
punishment_new: Express statutory codification of Zero-FIR (any police station) and Electronic FIR (e-FIR) with 3-day signature requirement.
explanation: CrPC Section 154 is now BNSS Section 173. For the first time, Zero FIR (registering crime irrespective of jurisdiction) and e-FIR (electronic filing) are explicitly written into the criminal procedural code.
source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023), Section 173

title: Procedure When Investigation Cannot be Completed in 24 Hours (Police Custody & Remand)
chapter: Information to Police and Powers to Investigate
old_text: The Magistrate may, whether he has or has not jurisdiction to try the case, from time to time, authorise the detention of the accused in such custody as such Magistrate thinks fit, for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole...
new_text: The Magistrate may authorize detention of the accused in police custody for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole, or in parts, at any time during the initial forty days or sixty days out of the total detention period of sixty days or ninety days.
punishment_old: Police custody limited to the first 15 days of arrest only.
punishment_new: Police custody of up to 15 days can now be granted in parts across the first 40 or 60 days of detention.
explanation: CrPC Section 167 moved to BNSS Section 187. In a major shift, police custody (capped at 15 days total) can now be sought in fragmented installments across the first 40 to 60 days of the remand period.
source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023), Section 187

title: When Bail May be Taken in Case of Non-Bailable Offence
chapter: Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
old_text: When any person accused of, or suspected of, the commission of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or appears or is brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, he may be released on bail...
new_text: When any person accused of, or suspected of, the commission of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or appears or is brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, he may be released on bail...
punishment_old: Magisterial bail powers subject to murder/life imprisonment bar.
punishment_new: Magisterial bail powers maintained under Section 480 BNSS.
explanation: CrPC Section 437 governing regular bail by Magistrates in non-bailable cases is renumbered as Section 480 of BNSS.
source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023), Section 480

title: Direction for Grant of Bail to Person Apprehending Arrest (Anticipatory Bail)
chapter: Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
old_text: Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail...
new_text: Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail...
punishment_old: Pre-arrest discretionary protection granted by Sessions Court or High Court.
punishment_new: Pre-arrest discretionary protection granted by Sessions Court or High Court.
explanation: Anticipatory bail moves from CrPC Section 438 to BNSS Section 482, preserving concurrent jurisdiction of the Sessions Court and High Court.
source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023), Section 482

title: Maximum Period for Which an Undertrial Prisoner Can Be Detained
chapter: Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
old_text: Where a person has, during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial under this Code of an offence under any law... undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence under that law, he shall be released by the Court on his personal bond...
new_text: Where a person has undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment... Provided that where such person is a first-time offender (who has never been convicted of any offence in the past), he shall be released on bond if he has undergone detention for one-third of the maximum period.
punishment_old: Release on bail mandatory upon completing one-half (50%) of maximum sentence.
punishment_new: First-time undertrials are entitled to mandatory bail upon completing one-third (33.3%) of the maximum sentence.
explanation: BNSS Section 479 significantly liberalizes undertrial relief: first-time offenders who have never been convicted before can now secure release on bail after serving only one-third of the statutory term instead of half.
source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023), Section 479
